Name: Prioritize and Plan the Account
Description: Decide where attention goes across accounts, workloads or solutions, and turn that decision into a plan someone can act on.
WhyItMatters: Time is the scarcest resource in the week. Deciding where it goes on evidence, rather than by habit or by whoever asked last, is the difference between a quarter you shaped and one that happened to you.
DesiredOutcome: A short, prioritized set of accounts, workloads or solution plays with a named next action and owner for each.
KeyTakeaway: Prioritization is a decision about what you will not do. AI can assemble the evidence; the choice stays yours.

Name: Inspect the Pipeline and Build the Forecast
Description: Inspect what the data says, correct what misrepresents reality, and build a forecast you can defend.
WhyItMatters: Every forecast conversation, coverage review and consumption call rests on data somebody has to trust. When the underlying signal is wrong, everything built on it is guesswork wearing a number.
DesiredOutcome: Corrected records and a defensible narrative that explains the position, the risk and what would close the gap.
KeyTakeaway: A forecast is an argument, not a number. AI improves the evidence; it does not make the call.

Name: Create and Qualify Demand
Description: Find the next real opportunity from signals already available, and qualify it on evidence rather than optimism.
WhyItMatters: Pipeline gaps are usually discovery gaps. The signals for the next opportunity are already sitting in accounts we own; the work is finding them on purpose rather than by luck.
DesiredOutcome: At least one new qualified opportunity with a documented trigger and a tested reason it is real.
KeyTakeaway: A pipeline gap is usually a discovery gap. Qualification is a test, not a stage.

Name: Prepare and Lead a Customer Conversation
Description: Prepare for the conversation that moves the decision, anticipate what will be asked, and lead it with evidence.
WhyItMatters: Customer conversations are where decisions actually move. They are won or lost in preparation, and preparation is the first thing dropped when the calendar fills.
DesiredOutcome: A prepared conversation with a stated intended outcome, the likely objections anticipated and the evidence ready.
KeyTakeaway: Preparation is where the meeting is decided. AI makes good preparation fast enough to actually happen.

Name: Design and Validate the Technical Solution
Description: Design the solution, then prove it works well enough for the customer to decide.
WhyItMatters: A design the customer cannot see or test is a document. Proof is what converts technical work into a customer decision, and criteria set afterwards get argued about forever.
DesiredOutcome: A validated design with explicit success and exit criteria the customer has agreed to.
KeyTakeaway: A design nobody has argued against has not been validated. Proof is what converts a design into a decision.

Name: Lead Discovery and Define Decision Criteria
Description: Understand the real problem and agree what would make the customer decide.
WhyItMatters: Discovery that ends without agreed decision criteria produces a second discovery meeting. The stated problem is rarely the real one.
DesiredOutcome: A bounded problem statement, named evidence gaps and written decision criteria.
KeyTakeaway: Discovery that does not end in decision criteria is a conversation, not discovery.

Name: Assess Health and Prioritize Risk
Description: Find the risk that matters most right now, and decide what to do about it while it is still cheap.
WhyItMatters: Risk found early is a conversation. The same risk found late is an escalation with an audience. Scores tell us something is wrong; they rarely tell us what to do.
DesiredOutcome: A ranked risk view with an owner, a date and one intervention already started.
KeyTakeaway: Risk found early is a conversation. The same risk found late is an escalation.

Name: Advance and Structure the Deal
Description: Move the deal to its next decision, and structure it so it can actually be approved.
WhyItMatters: Deals stall on structure more often than on merit. The cost of discovering an approval requirement late is measured in weeks.
DesiredOutcome: The next decision named, the blockers owned and a structure that can actually be approved.
KeyTakeaway: Deals stall on structure more often than on merit. Getting the shape right early is the cheapest work available.

Name: Prove and Communicate Value
Description: Turn what has actually happened into a value story the customer recognizes and will act on.
WhyItMatters: Value that is not evidenced reads as opinion, and value never communicated is invisible at renewal. Customers judge us on outcomes they can see.
DesiredOutcome: An evidence-based value story in the customer's own terms, with gaps named honestly.
KeyTakeaway: Value that is not evidenced is an opinion. Value that is not communicated is invisible.

Name: Manage Renewal and Expansion
Description: Protect the renewal and find the expansion that is already inside it.
WhyItMatters: A renewal is decided months before the date, usually by whether value was evidenced along the way. Expansion is easier to find inside a healthy renewal than outside one.
DesiredOutcome: A renewal position with the largest risk named and one evidenced expansion hypothesis.
KeyTakeaway: A renewal is decided months before the date. The work is in seeing the risk early enough to act.

Name: Orchestrate the Team, Partners and Delivery
Description: Get the right people moving on the right thing, and keep the handoffs clean enough to survive contact.
WhyItMatters: Most work stalls in the handoff, not the task. Account teams carry responsibility without authority, and explicit handoffs are the only reliable substitute.
DesiredOutcome: A mobilized team with a named owner, input and date for every handoff, and stalled items escalated.
KeyTakeaway: Most work stalls in the handoff, not in the task. Orchestration is making handoffs explicit.

Name: Validate Policy, Licensing and Compliance
Description: Check the deal against policy before policy checks the deal.
WhyItMatters: Policy questions found at approval cost weeks; found early they cost a conversation. Interpretation belongs to authoritative sources, never to assumption.
DesiredOutcome: A policy and licensing check with every open question routed to its authoritative owner.
KeyTakeaway: Policy questions found early are conversations. Found at approval, they are delays.

Name: Capture and Reuse What Works
Description: Turn work already done into something the team can find and reuse.
WhyItMatters: Teams routinely rebuild work that already exists because nobody could find the original. Reuse is the cheapest productivity available to us.
DesiredOutcome: One reusable asset captured with enough context that a colleague could pick it up unaided.
KeyTakeaway: Most teams rebuild artifacts that already exist. Reuse is the cheapest productivity available.

Name: Plan, Orchestrate and Realize Customer Investment
Description: Plan, request, deliver and prove the value of customer investment across the roles that touch it.
WhyItMatters: Customer investment succeeds or fails on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one link, and the chain breaks where the handoff is vague.
DesiredOutcome: An investment case moved to its next governed action, with the human decision and its owner named.
KeyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

Name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
Description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.
WhyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
DesiredOutcome: Every team member knows the format and the expectations, and leaves with one thing to try before the next session.
KeyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

Name: Identify and Test an AI-Assisted Workflow
Description: Surface a recurring workflow, choose the smallest useful AI-assisted step, and test it with clear evidence and human checkpoints.
WhyItMatters: Teams often wait for role-specific content when they could safely improve a real workflow using a reusable discovery and experiment pattern.
DesiredOutcome: A prioritized workflow opportunity and a bounded experiment with inputs, expected output, success evidence, owner, and human checkpoint.
KeyTakeaway: Start with the work, not the tool. A useful first experiment is narrow, observable, and easy to review.

Name: Transition an Account Without Losing the Customer
Description: Hand an account over so the incoming team keeps the relationship, the history and the open work, and the customer experiences continuity rather than a restart.
WhyItMatters: More than two thousand account transitions happen every year, and a poor one measurably depresses customer experience scores. The incoming seller inherits whatever the outgoing seller failed to write down, and the customer pays for the gap in repeated conversations they have already had.
DesiredOutcome: A completed transition where the customer has met the incoming team, the account plan and contacts are current, open pipeline has moved, and the ninety-day follow-up is owned.
KeyTakeaway: A transition is a customer experience before it is an administrative task. The record closes when the customer has been met, not when the fields are filled in.

Name: Hand Off Ownership Without Dropping the Customer
Description: Move ownership of an opportunity or milestone between the account, specialist and customer success teams so the receiving role can act immediately and the customer never repeats themselves.
WhyItMatters: Opportunities lose weeks in the space between two roles, and the customer experiences that gap as being asked the same questions by a new face. The transfer window is short precisely because the cost of a slow one lands on the customer.
DesiredOutcome: Ownership transferred within the expected window, with the qualification, milestone detail and customer context documented well enough that the receiving role starts from where you finished.
KeyTakeaway: A handoff is a gated transfer with exit criteria, not a notification. If the receiving role cannot act on what they were given, the handoff has not happened.

Name: Plan and Execute Consumption to Realized Usage
Description: Turn a customer commitment into a consumption plan with owned milestones, and drive those milestones through deployment to usage the customer actually gets value from.
WhyItMatters: Commitment without consumption is a renewal problem you have already paid for. The gap between what a customer agreed to spend and what they actually deploy is where accounts quietly go wrong, and it is visible long before it shows up in a number.
DesiredOutcome: A consumption plan with milestones that have owners, dates and evidence, and a clear read on which are progressing to usage and which are stalled.
KeyTakeaway: A signed commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. The plan is what converts one into the other, and it decays unless someone owns each milestone by name.

Name: Build and Govern Executive Sponsorship
Description: Map who actually decides, secure the executive relationships the account depends on, and keep them alive rather than rebuilding them every time something goes wrong.
WhyItMatters: Deals stall and escalations turn ugly at exactly the moment nobody senior on the customer side is invested enough to intervene. That investment is built over quarters and cannot be assembled in a week.
DesiredOutcome: A current map of who decides and who influences, an honest read on which relationships are real, and one specific action to deepen the sponsorship the account most depends on.
KeyTakeaway: An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship. Sponsorship is the relationship that already exists when you need it.

Name: Set Up the Fiscal Year and Defend the Territory Plan
Description: Turn a new fiscal year's quota, territory and account assignment into a coverage plan you can defend, and inspect it when the year is underway.
WhyItMatters: A territory plan that does not add up is discovered either in week three, when it is fixable, or in month nine, when it is not. The plan is also what you are held to, so it is worth being the person who found the gap first.
DesiredOutcome: A territory plan with the coverage gap quantified, the assumptions named, and the specific support requirements you will ask for.
KeyTakeaway: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number will come from. It is worth the hour it takes to find out whether that claim survives contact with the arithmetic.

Name: Land the Fiscal Year and Protect What Books
Description: Work out what can still book before the fiscal year closes, get the records right before the systems stop accepting changes, and tell the difference between a real deadline and a self-imposed one.
WhyItMatters: Year end is where a deal that was always going to close in July gets pushed into June and damaged, while a record that could have been corrected in a day quietly misses the cutoff. Knowing which is which is most of the skill.
DesiredOutcome: A short list of what can genuinely still book, the records that must be corrected before the systems close, and an honest separation of fiscal-dated work from deal-dated work.
KeyTakeaway: Almost nothing about June is a seller deadline. What is genuinely fixed is when the systems stop accepting changes, and that is the part most often discovered too late.

Name: Work the Signal Queue Before It Expires
Description: Take an inbound queue of marketing signals and plan priorities, decide fast which ones are real, and act on them inside the window rather than after it.
WhyItMatters: Signals arrive faster than anyone can work them, and the ones that expire do so silently. Whoever is deliberate about which signals they drop ends up ahead of whoever tries to work them all.
DesiredOutcome: A triaged signal queue with the expiring ones identified, a decision recorded on each, and one signal taken through to a qualified opportunity or deliberately closed.
KeyTakeaway: A signal is an unqualified lead with a clock on it. The skill is deciding quickly which ones deserve your time, not working all of them equally.

Name: Hand Work to a Partner and Keep It Moving
Description: Decide what genuinely belongs with a partner, hand it over with enough for them to act, and stay on it through the acceptance and conversion windows rather than assuming it landed.
WhyItMatters: Partner-led is structural in this segment rather than optional help, which means referrals that quietly expire are lost coverage you chose to give away. The difference between a partner motion that works and one that does not is almost entirely about what happens after the handoff.
DesiredOutcome: One referral packaged and sent with what the partner actually needs, a clear read on where your open referrals sit against their windows, and one stalled referral chased or closed.
KeyTakeaway: Handing something to a partner is not the end of your involvement. The windows run whether or not anyone is watching them, and the system closes the lead for you if nobody acts.

Name: Plan the Territory With the Partners Who Cover It
Description: Decide who is genuinely covering which accounts across a territory far larger than one person can work, and build that decision into a joint plan with the partners who cover the rest.
WhyItMatters: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be covered account by account, so most of it is covered by partners or not at all. The plan is where that becomes deliberate. Left implicit, the accounts that get worked are the ones that shout, and the ones that quietly lapse were never assigned to anybody.
DesiredOutcome: A territory segmented by who actually covers each account, the uncovered accounts named rather than assumed, and one joint plan input ready for the partner conversation.
KeyTakeaway: Coverage is a decision whether or not you make it. An account nobody named is an account nobody is working.

Name: Earn Customer Satisfaction on Every Delivery
Description: Treat customer satisfaction as something evidenced and acted on during delivery, rather than discovered when the survey comes back.
WhyItMatters: A low score is rarely a surprise to the customer, only to us. The dissatisfaction was visible during delivery, and nobody named it while there was still time to act.
DesiredOutcome: One satisfaction risk named with evidence, and one action taken before the survey window closes.
KeyTakeaway: Satisfaction is decided long before the survey. The signals are there during delivery if you go looking for them.

Name: Build the Technical Credibility the Role Depends On
Description: Close the distance between what the customer needs you to be credible on and what you can speak to today, deliberately rather than accidentally.
WhyItMatters: Customers decide early whether you are the person they call. That decision rests on whether you can speak to what they are building, not on your title.
DesiredOutcome: One named gap between what the customer will need and what you can currently defend, with a specific way to close it.
KeyTakeaway: Technical credibility is the currency of the role. It gets built on purpose or not at all.

Name: Design and Validate the Technical Solution
Description: Design the solution, then prove it works well enough for the customer to decide.
WhyItMatters: A design the customer cannot see or test is a document. Proof is what converts technical work into a customer decision, and criteria set afterwards get argued about forever.
DesiredOutcome: A validated design with explicit success and exit criteria the customer has agreed to.
KeyTakeaway: A design nobody has argued against has not been validated. Proof is what converts a design into a decision.
